\chapter{The Stick at the End}
\label{ch:sa-the-stick-at-the-end}
\hlchaptermodality{60}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read and write the daṇḍa that ends a Sanskrit sentence, and say what classical Sanskrit punctuates with instead of the marks English uses.}

Complete SA-C60-danda and say what a single stroke marks and what a doubled one marks.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[daṇḍa]{\sk{।} — the daṇḍa}

\label{lesson:SA-C60-danda}



\begin{quote}
Answer \textbf{\sk{कुतः}} out loud. You have been reading Sanskrit sentences for fifty-nine chapters. Nobody has told you how one ends.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: the whole of Sanskrit punctuation}
\textbf{\sk{।}} — the \textbf{daṇḍa}, \textquotedblleft{}the stick\textquotedblright{}.

One vertical stroke, drawn from the headline down. It marks the end of a sentence, and it is very nearly the entire punctuation system of classical Sanskrit.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{सः} \sk{भारतात्} \sk{आगच्छति।}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{यः} \sk{गच्छति} \sk{सः} \sk{पश्यति।}}
\end{quote}

Doubled — \textbf{\sk{॥}} — it closes a verse, and the pair of strokes is what you see at the end of every line of a printed śloka.

What is worth noticing is everything the list does \textbf{not} contain. Classical Sanskrit has no comma, no colon, no brackets, no quotation marks, no question mark and no exclamation mark. Where English reaches for punctuation, Sanskrit reaches for a word: you met \textbf{\sk{इति}} two chapters ago closing a quotation that no quotation mark was ever going to close, and \textbf{\sk{किम्}} at the front of a sentence does the work of a question mark.

That is not a gap in the writing system. It is a different division of labour — the grammar carries what the marks carry in English, and one stick is enough for the rest.

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{।}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} draw a single vertical stroke top-to-bottom, the height of a letter, just after the last letter of the sentence
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 0.} The stroke is one movement and there is nothing to add to it.

\begin{quote}
The daṇḍa is a mark of punctuation rather than a letter: it carries no sound, takes no vowel sign, and never joins to what stands beside it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find the mark that ends it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{यः} \sk{गच्छति} \sk{सः} \sk{पश्यति।}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{\sk{।}} three times
  \item \emph{Say it:} three things English punctuates that Sanskrit does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\sk{।}} mark, and what does \textbf{\sk{॥}} mark? (The end of a sentence, and the end of a verse.)
